Prefill-decode disaggregation separates the two computationally distinct phases of LLM inference onto dedicated accelerator pools: prefill nodes handle the compute-intensive KV cache population for incoming prompts, while decode nodes handle the memory-bandwidth-bound token generation. The central question is how to schedule work across these pools when prompt lengths are not fixed — because a 128-token prompt and a 4096-token prompt impose radically different prefill durations, and if decode nodes are consuming KV cache at a rate mismatched to prefill node throughput, you get either starvation (decode nodes idle, waiting for KV transfers) or backpressure accumulation (prefill queue depth explodes). The heterogeneous accelerator memory bandwidth dimension compounds this: if your prefill fleet runs on A100s and your decode fleet on L40S cards with different HBM bandwidth profiles, the KV cache transfer time across the interconnect (NVLink, PCIe, or RDMA over InfiniBand) becomes a non-deterministic bottleneck that the scheduler must model without actually observing until after the fact. What a beginner misses is that the instability is not just a throughput problem but a latency tail problem — under a heavy-tailed prompt length distribution (which production traffic almost always exhibits), the p99 prefill latency for long prompts can saturate the transfer channel exactly when the decode pool is most starved, creating a resonance condition where queue depth oscillates rather than converges. Experts worry specifically about the feedback loop: naive schedulers that throttle prefill admission to protect decode latency end up increasing mean prefill queue depth, which raises KV cache memory pressure on prefill nodes, which forces eviction of partially-computed states and re-computation — a cascade that simple throughput metrics will not reveal until SLA breach is already underway.

The dominant determinant is whether KV cache transfer is push-based or pull-based: in push-based designs (prefill node initiates RDMA write to decode node memory as soon as a sequence completes), a burst of long prompts causes a thundering-herd write storm that saturates the interconnect precisely when decode nodes are already congested, amplifying oscillation; pull-based designs (decode node requests KV blocks when it has capacity) naturally rate-limit transfer to decode-side absorption capacity, providing a damping mechanism at the cost of added latency per sequence. Transfer granularity matters critically — systems that transfer the entire KV tensor for a completed sequence atomically (as in the original Splitwise paper, Pratyush Patel et al., 2023) create bursty, high-variance transfer events, whereas chunked or pipelined transfer (sending KV layers as they complete, overlapping with remaining prefill computation) smooths the injection rate but requires the decode node to begin partial token generation with incomplete cache state, which most current implementations do not support. The interconnect's bandwidth-delay product sets the oscillation frequency: over NVLink with ~600 GB/s aggregate bandwidth, a 4096-token, 70B-parameter KV tensor (~2 GB in FP16 per layer across 80 layers) transfers in roughly 3–4ms, meaning scheduling decisions made on a coarser timescale than this window will systematically mis-estimate decode-node readiness. Flow control at the RDMA layer is particularly treacherous — RoCEv2 with Priority Flow Control (PFC) can introduce head-of-line blocking when long-prompt KV transfers monopolize a priority queue, causing short-prompt sequences (which should complete quickly) to stall behind them, inverting the intended latency ordering. DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024) demonstrated that even with careful disaggregation, the ratio of prefill-to-decode node allocation must be tuned per workload distribution, and a mismatch of even 1.5× in this ratio under bursty long-prompt traffic shifts the system from a stable operating point into oscillating underutilization on decode nodes alternating with transfer-channel saturation.

The foundational primitive is sequence-priority-tagged transfer queues on the prefill node: completed KV tensors are not immediately injected into the transfer channel but instead enqueued with a priority derived from the decode node's current queue depth for that sequence class, allowing short-sequence KV transfers (small tensors, low channel occupancy) to preempt in-flight long-sequence transfers — this requires RDMA implementations that support mid-stream preemption or, more practically, chunked transfer with per-chunk priority re-evaluation at chunk boundaries. A complementary primitive is admission-coupled transfer throttling: the prefill scheduler maintains a token bucket per decode node that is refilled at the rate the decode node signals it is consuming completed sequences (via lightweight heartbeat acknowledgments), and KV transfer initiation is gated on available tokens — this converts the push model into a quasi-pull model without the full round-trip latency of true pull, and IBM Research's work on disaggregated inference scheduling (circa 2024) explored similar backpressure signaling though without the per-class priority layer. Speculative KV pre-staging offers a third lever: for short sequences whose prefill completes while a long-sequence transfer is occupying the channel, the prefill node writes the short-sequence KV tensor to a local NVME or CPU-DRAM staging buffer and signals the decode node that the tensor is available-but-not-yet-transferred; the decode node can then initiate a pull at its next scheduling quantum, decoupling transfer timing from prefill completion and eliminating the starvation window. The critical implementation constraint is that all three primitives require per-sequence state tracking on the prefill node beyond what most current systems maintain — Mooncake (Qin et al., 2024) moves toward this by treating the KV cache as a disaggregated object store with explicit lifecycle management, but does not yet expose priority-aware transfer scheduling as a first-class API. The non-obvious danger in combining these primitives is priority inversion under sustained load: if short sequences are always preempting long-sequence transfers, long sequences accumulate in the staging buffer, their KV tensors consume prefill-node HBM, and eventually the prefill node must either evict (forcing recomputation) or block new prefill admissions — so the throttling policy must include an aging mechanism that gradually elevates long-sequence transfer priority as their staging dwell time increases, analogous to the aging heuristics in classical OS scheduling but operating on sub-100ms timescales.

The minimum state required to make recomputation cheaper than full re-prefill is layer-boundary activation checkpoints: if the prefill node retains the residual stream tensor at a set of layer boundaries (e.g., every 8 layers in a 80-layer model), evicting the KV tensors for intermediate layers only requires recomputing those layers rather than the full forward pass — for a 70B model at FP16, a full residual stream at one layer boundary costs roughly 2 × sequence_length × hidden_dim × 2 bytes, so for a 4096-token sequence with hidden dim 8192 that's ~134 MB per checkpoint, meaning 10 checkpoints costs ~1.3 GB versus ~16 GB for the full KV cache, a favorable tradeoff if recomputation FLOPS are cheaper than re-ingesting the prompt tokens. The critical additional piece is the attention mask and position encoding state: rotary position embeddings (RoPE) are recomputed cheaply from token positions alone, but ALiBi or learned absolute position embeddings require either recomputation from the original input token sequence or storing the position bias tensors explicitly — this makes retaining the original token ID sequence (a few KB) essential metadata even when all activation state is evicted. Prefix sharing complicates this significantly: if the evicted sequence shared a KV prefix with other live sequences (as in systems using RadixAttention from SGLang, Zheng et al., 2024), evicting its unique-suffix KV tensor is straightforward, but the shared prefix KV blocks cannot be evicted without harming all co-tenants, so the recomputation saving only applies to the suffix portion, and the checkpoint must record exactly where the shared prefix ends. The architectural features that close off cheaper recomputation are sliding window attention (as in Mistral-style models) and state space model hybrid layers (as in Mamba or Jamba): sliding window attention means intermediate activations cannot be reconstructed from layer-boundary residuals alone because the attention computation at layer L depends on a bounded local KV window that was never fully materialized as a storable tensor, while SSM layers maintain a recurrent hidden state that is order-dependent and cannot be recomputed from a later checkpoint without replaying all preceding tokens through the SSM kernel. Cross-attention layers in encoder-decoder architectures present a related problem: the cross-attention KV tensors are derived from the encoder output, not the decoder residual stream, so a checkpoint-based recovery scheme must either retain the encoder output separately or treat cross-attention KV eviction as unrecoverable without full encoder re-inference, which for long documents can dominate total recomputation cost.

The first intervention is prefill admission gating with backpressure propagation: the prefill node stops accepting new sequences from the request router until HBM pressure drops below a threshold, effectively trading increased queue depth at the router for preserved in-flight state integrity — this requires the router to have a meaningful backpressure signal (not just TCP buffer fullness but explicit HBM occupancy metrics), which systems like Kubernetes-based inference controllers rarely expose at sub-second granularity, making this intervention harder to implement cleanly than it sounds. A more surgical option is in-flight prefill preemption with partial-result parking: if a long sequence is currently mid-prefill and consuming HBM as its KV and SSM states accumulate layer by layer, the scheduler can pause that sequence's prefill at the current layer boundary, serialize the accumulated state to CPU DRAM or NVMe (at PCIe 4.0 bandwidth of ~28 GB/s, parking 4 GB of state takes ~140ms), and immediately reclaim its HBM for the sequences whose states are fully computed and awaiting transfer — this sacrifices latency for one sequence to prevent cascade eviction across many. Sequence migration to a less-pressured prefill node is the third lever, and the most operationally complex: if the cluster has multiple prefill nodes and the dependency graph is locked, transferring both the partial state and the remaining token sequence to a peer node with available HBM avoids local eviction entirely, but requires atomic handoff of the partial SSM state mid-computation, which no current production system implements — Mooncake's disaggregated KV store architecture (Qin et al., 2024) provides the object store substrate this would require but stops short of live migration of incomplete prefill state. A fourth, underappreciated intervention is prompt truncation with semantic suffix dropping: for sequences where the prompt has a structured format (system prompt + context + query), the prefill node can negotiate with the request layer to drop lower-priority context segments, resubmit a shorter prompt, and free HBM without eviction — this requires the serving stack to expose prompt segmentation metadata to the prefill scheduler, which systems like SGLang begin to support through its structured prompt APIs but only for prefix-cacheable segments, not arbitrary truncation. The intervention that practitioners most often overlook is decode-side pull acceleration: rather than manipulating the prefill node's memory, the scheduler signals decode nodes to immediately pull any completed KV tensors currently staged in prefill HBM, even if the decode node's local queue is not yet empty — this converts prefill HBM from a staging buffer back into working memory, and if even two or three completed sequences can be flushed this way, the freed HBM often resolves the pressure without any preemption or migration.

Bidirectional backpressure — prefill nodes unable to flush because decode nodes are full, decode nodes unable to accept because prefill nodes cannot deliver new completed sequences fast enough to replace finishing ones — reveals that static prefill-to-decode ratios are fundamentally assumptions about workload stationarity that production traffic violates continuously; the ratio that DistServe (Zhong et al., 2024) identifies as optimal for a given prompt/output length distribution becomes actively harmful the moment that distribution shifts, because neither pool can shed load to the other and the system locks into a state where both pools are simultaneously saturated and starved. The deeper structural problem is that prefill and decode have asymmetric scaling curves: adding one prefill node gives roughly linear throughput gains for compute-bound long prompts, while adding one decode node gives sublinear gains under memory-bandwidth saturation because the KV cache access pattern across many concurrent sequences is increasingly random, not sequential — so a naive autoscaler that adds nodes proportionally to queue depth will consistently overprovision decode and underprovision prefill under heavy long-prompt bursts, the exact condition that created the bidirectional backpressure in the first place. A well-designed autoscaler must therefore monitor transfer channel utilization as a leading indicator rather than queue depth as a lagging one: when NVLink or RDMA channel utilization between prefill and decode pools exceeds ~70% sustained for more than 5–10 seconds, this predicts bidirectional saturation 20–40 seconds before queue depth metrics cross alert thresholds, giving the autoscaler a meaningful reaction window — Google's Pathways serving infrastructure uses similar predictive signals though the specifics are not fully published. The autoscaler's correct response is asymmetric and staged: first, add prefill nodes (which can begin serving new short sequences immediately, reducing incoming HBM pressure on existing prefill nodes without requiring KV transfer channel capacity); second, only add decode nodes after confirming the transfer channel is the bottleneck rather than decode-side compute, because prematurely adding decode nodes increases KV pull demand and can worsen channel saturation before it improves throughput. The fundamental limit exposed here is that disaggregated inference requires the autoscaler to treat the transfer channel as a first-class resource with its own capacity dimension, not merely a consequence of node counts — current Kubernetes-based autoscalers operating on CPU/GPU utilization metrics have no native abstraction for inter-node bandwidth as a schedulable resource, meaning clusters running disaggregated inference on RoCEv2 fabrics with finite oversubscription ratios will repeatedly hit this failure mode until the orchestration layer is extended with bandwidth-aware scheduling primitives analogous to what network-aware schedulers like Volcano or Koordinator have begun to approximate for training workloads.

The most effective immediate intervention is priority-stratified queue shedding with client-visible backpressure: rather than accepting all requests into an internal queue that will breach latency SLAs invisibly, the serving layer returns HTTP 429s with Retry-After headers to the lowest-priority request tier the moment internal queue depth crosses a threshold calibrated to the provisioning latency — for a 90-second provisioning gap at typical arrival rates, this threshold should be set conservatively enough that the queue does not grow beyond what existing nodes can drain in 90 seconds at sustained throughput, which requires knowing per-sequence expected decode length, something most routers approximate poorly. Prompt length-based admission tiering provides a more surgical alternative to flat shedding: the serving layer classifies incoming requests by estimated prefill cost (using a lightweight length predictor or simply the token count) and admits short sequences freely while gating long sequences behind a separate queue with explicit capacity limits — this asymmetry is justified because short sequences cycle through prefill and decode quickly, freeing resources within the provisioning window, while long sequences consume HBM for the entire gap duration and are the direct cause of the saturation condition. A third strategy is speculative decode acceleration for in-flight sequences: during the provisioning gap, decode nodes can increase speculative decoding draft length (e.g., from 4 to 8 draft tokens per step using a smaller draft model) to improve tokens-per-second on already-admitted sequences, draining the decode queue faster and creating HBM headroom — this trades draft model compute cost for reduced decode-node occupancy time, and systems like Medusa (Cai et al., 2024) show that longer draft sequences can improve throughput by 30–50% under low-rejection-rate conditions, though this degrades if the traffic distribution shifts the acceptance rate. Ephemeral CPU-DRAM KV offload serves as a pressure relief valve specifically for the prefill-to-decode transfer bottleneck: completed KV tensors that cannot immediately transfer to saturated decode nodes are written to prefill-node CPU DRAM (typically 1–2 TB available on modern GPU servers) via PCIe, freeing HBM for new prefill work, with decode nodes pulling from CPU DRAM when their HBM has capacity — the latency penalty of CPU-DRAM-resident KV access is significant (PCIe bandwidth ~28–64 GB/s versus HBM's ~3 TB/s), but this is preferable to re-prefill or SLA breach during a 90-second window. The intervention practitioners most consistently underinvest in is pre-provisioning warm standby capacity scaled to historical burst variance: if traffic logs show that bidirectional backpressure events occur with a 20-minute periodicity (common in diurnal patterns), maintaining one warm standby prefill node and one decode node in a suspended state that can activate in under 10 seconds eliminates the provisioning gap entirely for predictable bursts, at a cost of roughly 10–15% idle GPU overhead — this is cheaper than the SLA penalty credits triggered by cascading violations during provisioning gaps, a tradeoff that becomes obvious in postmortem analysis but is rarely made proactively.
